newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Talks on Czech cabinet reshuffle to resume Monday.
newsitem.headline: Talks on Czech cabinet reshuffle to resume Monday.

text.p: Leaders of the three-party ruling Czech coalition will meet on Monday morning to continue discussions on restructuring the cabinet after the reesignation of three ministers over the weekend, the Czech news agency CTK reported on Sunday
"The content of the meeting will be changes in the government and other areas of cooperation within the coalition," CTK quoted Civic Democratic Party (ODS) spokeswoman Jana Petrova as saying.

The leaderships of the three parties in the centre-right coalition have been meeting separately this weekend to discuss changes in the cabinet, aimed at shoring up support for Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's government which has been battered by worsening economic news.
Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik, Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy, and Interior Minister Jan Ruml all announced their resignations on Saturday.

But the waters were muddied by President Vaclav Havel, who said in a radio interview recorded before the resignations were announced that individual ministers should not be sacrificed without the government discussing the situation thoroughly.
Klaus agreed with his coalition partners on Wednesday that a change was needed amid slumping approval ratings and an economic downturn which has sapped confidence in the government.
The cabinet shuffle has become even more sensitive as pressure mounts on the Czech crown, which has been hit by foreign speculators reacting to poor macroeconomic results and political instability.

Klaus told a news conference on Saturday that 52-year-old Kocarnik, a member of his Civic Democratic Party (ODS), would be replaced by the premier's chief adviser Jiri Waigel, an economist who is not affiliated to any party.

Calls began for Kocarnik to go last year after a rash of financial scandals which resulted in the fall of a number of banks, and intensified earlier this year when the government agreed on a set of spending cuts to avoid a budget deficit.
